issues.legal_issue: A state law may vest ownership of mineral rights in the state without being repugnant to central legislation regulating mines and mineral development when the central law contemplates state vesting and does not itself acquire ownership of the land.
material_facts: The state enacted a law authorizing it to acquire rights to minerals in land, including saltpetre deposits, and issued notifications under that law.
The central legislation regulated mining and mineral development and the grant of mining rights, but did not acquire ownership of mineral-bearing land.

The central legislation required certain mining leases in land vested in a state to be brought into conformity with its provisions, and separately contemplated central mining operations on land in which minerals vested in a state or another person.
The state law made its operation subject to the central legislation.
issues.conclusion: The state law was valid and not repugnant to the central legislation; the state could validly acquire ownership rights in the mineral deposits.
issues.legal_principle: The character of legislation is determined by the substance and effect of its operative provisions, not merely by its stated objects and reasons. The central law's declaration under section 2 must be read with its provisions, including sections 16(1)(b) and 17: those provisions contemplate state vesting of mineral-bearing land while requiring mining rights to be governed by the central law. The central law did not occupy the separate field of acquiring ownership of the land. The Court distinguished the circumstances addressed in Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa, State of West Bengal v. Union of India, State of Orissa v. M. A. Tulloch & Co., and Baijnath Kedia v. State of Bihar, particularly because the central law had been amended after the earlier decisions.

rule.if: state_legislation_validity_challenge and state_law_vests_mineral_ownership and central_law_regulates_mining_rights and (central_law_contemplates_state_vesting or central_law_leaves_land_acquisition_unaddressed)

predicates.state_legislation_validity_challenge: A party challenges the validity of state legislation that concerns mineral-bearing land.
predicates.state_law_vests_mineral_ownership: The state law authorizes the state to acquire ownership of mineral rights in land.
predicates.central_law_regulates_mining_rights: The central law regulates mining operations or the grant of mining rights.
predicates.central_law_contemplates_state_vesting: The central law provides for mining rights in land that has vested in a state to be governed by the central regulatory scheme.
predicates.central_law_leaves_land_acquisition_unad: The central law regulates mining but does not itself acquire ownership of the mineral-bearing land.

issues.definition: When a validity challenge concerns a state law vesting mineral ownership and the central law regulates mining rights while contemplating state vesting or leaving land acquisition unaddressed, the state vesting law is not repugnant.

issues.legal_issue: Acquisition of ownership of mineral rights does not by itself terminate subsisting mining lease or licence rights governed by central law.
material_facts: The state law acquired proprietary rights to mineral deposits but did not mention leasehold or licence rights.
The state law expressly made the state's powers subject to the central legislation.
The central legislation required certain existing mining leases in vested land to be brought into conformity with its provisions.

The petitioners asserted that they held mining leases, but the Court was not shown that any particular petitioner had a subsisting right governed by the central legislation or that the challenged notifications affected such a right.
issues.conclusion: Subsisting mining lease or licence rights governed by the central legislation could continue despite the acquisition of mineral ownership, but the petitioners had not established such rights in these proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: The state law's acquisition of proprietary rights did not ipso facto terminate lease or licence rights governed by the central law. Section 3(2) of the state law made it subject to the central law, and section 16, as amended by the 1972 legislation, required qualifying existing leases to be brought into conformity with the central regime. Accordingly, established rights governed by that regime could continue, although an applicant must show that such rights subsist and are affected.

predicates.mineral_rights_case: The dispute concerns mineral ownership and mining rights in land.
predicates.subsisting_mining_rights_governed_by_cen: A mining lease or licence is still in force and is governed by the central regulatory scheme.

issues.definition: If a mineral-rights dispute involves a subsisting mining lease or licence governed by the central scheme, that right continues despite vesting of mineral ownership.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant seeking relief against action affecting mining rights must establish a subsisting right governed by the applicable mining law and show how the challenged action affects it.
material_facts: The petitioners came to court as lessees rather than as owners of the mineral rights.
They did not establish that their leases were governed by, or had been brought into conformity with, the central legislation.
The petitions and supporting materials did not show how the challenged acquisition or auction notifications affected any particular subsisting lease or licence right.
The Court stated that a claimant able to establish such a right could pursue any proceedings still available under law.
issues.conclusion: The claims were dismissed as framed because the petitioners had not established an affected subsisting right, without foreclosing appropriate proceedings by a claimant who could establish such a right.
issues.legal_principle: A party seeking judicial relief must plead and establish the right said to be infringed and the connection between that right and the challenged action. The Court found the essential averments needed to establish subsisting rights and the petitioners' entitlement to relief wanting, while leaving open appropriate proceedings for anyone able to prove a right governed by the central law.

predicates.writ_challenge_to_mining_action: A claimant seeks writ relief challenging government action concerning mineral rights or mining.
predicates.claimant_asserts_lease_right: The claimant relies on a mining lease rather than claiming ownership of the mineral rights.
predicates.establishes_affected_subsisting_regulate: The claimant proves a subsisting right governed by the applicable mining law and shows that the challenged action affects it.

issues.definition: When a claimant relying on a lease challenges mining-related government action but does not establish an affected subsisting regulated right, the present claim is dismissed without preventing proceedings based on a proven right.

issues.legal_issue: A person seeking mandamus should ordinarily first call on the authority to perform its legal obligation and allow a reasonable time for refusal or neglect before applying to court.
material_facts: The petitioners sought relief in the nature of mandamus against the state authorities.
The Court was not shown that any claimant had first asked the authority to perform the alleged statutory or contractual obligation before invoking writ jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: A claimant seeking mandamus should ordinarily make a prior demand and show that the authority refused or neglected to act within a reasonable time.
issues.legal_principle: As a well-known rule of practice, an applicant for mandamus should ordinarily first call upon the concerned authority to discharge its legal obligation and show refusal or neglect within a reasonable time, even where the alleged obligation is established.

predicates.mandamus_sought: A claimant applies to a court for an order requiring an authority to perform an alleged legal obligation.
predicates.prior_demand_followed_by_refusal_or_negl: The claimant first asks the authority to act and the authority then refuses or neglects to act within a reasonable time.

issues.definition: When mandamus is sought without a prior demand followed by refusal or neglect, the ordinary practice requires that demand and noncompliance before the order is sought.

issues.legal_issue: A statement of objects and reasons may assist when an enactment's purpose is disputed or uncertain, but it cannot override clear operative statutory language.
material_facts: The parties disputed the purpose and effect of the state enactment concerning mineral rights.
The enactment's operative provisions expressly addressed acquisition of proprietary mineral rights and did not mention leasehold or licence rights.
issues.conclusion: The enactment's effect had to be determined from its substantive provisions; its statement of objects and reasons could not override their clear language.
issues.legal_principle: A statement of objects and reasons is not part of the statute and may be relevant when the object or purpose is disputed or uncertain. It cannot override the effect that follows from explicit and unmistakable operative language, which is the best evidence of legislative intention.

predicates.statutory_interpretation_case: A court must determine the meaning or effect of an enactment.
predicates.operative_language_is_unambiguous: The enactment's operative provisions express their effect clearly and unmistakably.

issues.definition: In statutory interpretation, clear operative language controls over a statement of objects and reasons.

issues.legal_issue: A court deciding a pending case must apply the law as it exists at the time of decision and may hear arguments about the effect of an intervening amendment on an issue already before it.
material_facts: The central legislation had been amended while the appeals and petitions were pending.
The Court invited further argument about how the amended provisions affected the question already under consideration.
A party objected that considering those arguments would allow a new question to be raised.
issues.conclusion: Considering the effect of the amended law on the existing issue did not amount to allowing a new question; the Court was required to apply the law as it then existed.
issues.legal_principle: Courts take judicial notice of the law as it exists and must apply current law rather than law as it once was. Allowing the parties to address the effect of an amendment on the same issue does not, for that reason alone, permit a new question to be raised.

predicates.pending_case_involves_existing_issue: A case is pending before a court on an issue already placed before it.
predicates.governing_law_changed_before_decision: The law relevant to that issue changes before the court decides the case.

issues.definition: When the governing law changes while a case on an existing issue is pending, the court applies current law and may consider its effect on that issue.
